newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel official slams exchange rate regime.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel official slams exchange rate regime.

text.p: A top Bank of Israel official said in a paper released on Tuesday the current exchange rate system, featuring a fixed trading band to control shekel movement, hurts the economy.

"We are telling anyone who will listen: the present situation whereby the Bank of Israel buys large amounts of foreign currency because of the commitment placed on it to maintain the (shekel) trading band, hurts market mechanisms and the economy," David Klein wrote.
Klein, director of the central bank's monetary division, called for a more flexible exchange rate regime.
"Exchange rate regimes are not inscribed in the Ten Commandments...but man-made and must be adapted to changing circumstances."

Current exchange rate policy allows the shekel to fluctuate in a trading band of seven percent above or below a sloping mid-point designed to devalue the Israeli currency at a rate of six percent a year against a basket of key foreign currencies.
The Bank of Israel said recently it had been forced to intervene heavily in the currency market, buying $5 billion this year to prevent the shekel from appreciating above the trading band.
"As long as this (need for such intervention)...continues, the damage and price the economy will pay will increase and the way out will be more costly," Klein wrote.
Klein suggested loosening foreign currency regulations for Israelis by allowing private individuals to hold foreign currency accounts in local banks.

"As for the business sector, it is possible to cancel all remaining remnants of exchange control," he said. "There is no reason the Israeli economy cannot by the end of the decade be like all the developed markets and have a completely convertible currency."

The Bank of Israel and the Treasury have been discussing a foreign currency liberalisation programme but officials said final proposals have been delayed by differences mainly over rules for investment abroad by Israeli financial institutions. - Jerusalem newsroom, 972-2-5370502
